action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete'; omitted means 'publish'. What each does and takes is under **Calls** in the description.

file_path.description: publish: the local page to publish (.html; .md only when a skill says so); with `asset: true`, the local file to upload. A short, distinctive basename doubles as the last-resort title.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page (see **Calls**).

favicon.description: Browser-tab icon: one or two emoji (e.g. "📊"). No markup. Required on a page's first publish; omit on a redeploy (same file path this session, or `url`) to keep the artifact's icon — pass a new one only when the user asks.

limit.description: list only: maximum artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing — 'mine' (default), 'shared', 'all', 'assets' (with `url`; `after` continues it); see **Calls**.

title.description: publish: fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title> (a name, not a summary; keep it stable across redeploys).

description.description: publish: one sentence for the gallery card's subtitle.

label.description: A short name for the version this publish makes, max 60 chars (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Shown in the version picker. Optional — a few words, not a description.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai URL: on a publish, the artifact to update in place (one the user owns; omit for a new artifact or a same-conversation redeploy — see **To update an artifact from an earlier conversation**); for read, delete and the other url-addressed calls, the artifact to act on.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the user: what you need from it, to steer the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: last-resort overwrite that DISCARDS the newer published version (another session's publish, or someone's save from the page). On a conflict the fix is to merge your changes onto the newer content (handed to you in the rejection, or re-read) and publish again — not force. Pass true only when the user explicitly said to discard that specific version; the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with an asset id as `path`: directory to save the file into (default: the working directory); the file is named by the asset id plus the extension for its type.

path.description: read: an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result) — that asset is saved to a local file.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, to continue it.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config} — load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. Omit on a redeploy to keep what the page has; {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version — omit to keep it (the default), 'latest' to upgrade, an exact version to pin or roll back. Changes how the published page behaves: pass only when the author explicitly intends that.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide

Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

@@ -0,0 +1,81 @@
+package gitrepo
+
+import (
+	"bytes"
+	"context"
+	"fmt"
+	"os/exec"
+
+	"github.com/go-git/go-git/v6/plumbing"
+)
+
+// ChangedWorktreeFiles reports which paths differ between commit and the
+// working tree, using native Git's clean-filter semantics. It compares against
+// commit rather than the index because callers may run after the index has
+// moved on to content that is not part of that commit.
+//
+// The paths must be repository-relative. They are passed as literal pathspecs,
+// so filenames that look like pathspec magic remain filenames. Large path sets
+// are split across commands because git diff has no --pathspec-from-file option
+// and an oversized argv would fail before Git could inspect anything.
+func ChangedWorktreeFiles(
+	ctx context.Context,
+	worktreeRoot string,
+	commit plumbing.Hash,
+	paths []string,
+) (map[string]struct{}, error) {
+	changed := make(map[string]struct{})
+	if len(paths) == 0 {
+		return changed, nil
+	}
+
+	baseArgs := []string{
+		"--no-optional-locks", "-C", worktreeRoot,
+		"diff", "--name-only", "-z", "--no-renames", "--no-ext-diff", "--no-textconv",
+		commit.String(), "--",
+	}
+	for _, pathspecs := range chunkLiteralPathspecs(paths, gitDiffPathspecBudget) {
+		args := append(append([]string(nil), baseArgs...), pathspecs...)
+		cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", args...)
+		cmd.Env = EnvWithoutRepoOverrides()
+		out, err := cmd.Output()
+		if err != nil {
+			return nil, fmt.Errorf("git diff working tree against %s: %w", commit, err)
+		}
+
+		for entry := range bytes.SplitSeq(out, []byte{0}) {
+			if len(entry) != 0 {
+				changed[string(entry)] = struct{}{}
+			}
+		}
+	}
+	return changed, nil
+}
+
+// Keep pathspec argv comfortably below Windows' 32 KiB command-line limit,
+// including room for fixed arguments and os/exec quoting. Unix limits are much
+// larger. A single repository-relative path can exceed the budget and is sent
+// alone; filesystem path limits still keep that command bounded.
+const gitDiffPathspecBudget = 8 * 1024
+
+func chunkLiteralPathspecs(paths []string, budget int) [][]string {
+	var chunks [][]string
+	var (
+		chunk []string
+		size  int
+	)
+	for _, path := range paths {
+		pathspec := ":(literal)" + path
+		if len(chunk) > 0 && size+len(pathspec)+1 > budget {
+			chunks = append(chunks, chunk)
+			chunk = nil
+			size = 0
+		}
+		chunk = append(chunk, pathspec)
+		size += len(pathspec) + 1
+	}
+	if len(chunk) > 0 {
+		chunks = append(chunks, chunk)
+	}
+	return chunks
+}

+package gitrepo
+
+import (
+	"slices"
+	"strings"
+	"testing"
+)
+
+func TestChunkLiteralPathspecsBoundsCommandsWithoutDroppingPaths(t *testing.T) {
+	t.Parallel()
+
+	paths := []string{
+		strings.Repeat("a", 40),
+		strings.Repeat("b", 40),
+		strings.Repeat("c", 120), // A single path larger than the budget stays alone.
+		strings.Repeat("d", 40),
+	}
+	const budget = 100
+	chunks := chunkLiteralPathspecs(paths, budget)
+
+	var got []string
+	for _, chunk := range chunks {
+		var size int
+		for _, pathspec := range chunk {
+			got = append(got, strings.TrimPrefix(pathspec, ":(literal)"))
+			size += len(pathspec) + 1
+		}
+		if len(chunk) > 1 && size > budget {
+			t.Fatalf("multi-path chunk has size %d, budget %d", size, budget)
+		}
+	}
+	if !slices.Equal(got, paths) {
+		t.Fatalf("chunked paths = %q, want %q", got, paths)
+	}
+}

+package gitrepo
+
+import (
+	"bytes"
+	"context"
+	"fmt"
+	"os/exec"
+
+	"github.com/go-git/go-git/v6/plumbing"
+)
+
+// ChangedWorktreeFiles reports which paths differ between commit and the
+// working tree, using native Git's clean-filter semantics. It compares against
+// commit rather than the index because callers may run after the index has
+// moved on to content that is not part of that commit.
+//
+// The paths must be repository-relative. They are passed as literal pathspecs,
+// so filenames that look like pathspec magic remain filenames. Large path sets
+// are split across commands because git diff has no --pathspec-from-file option
+// and an oversized argv would fail before Git could inspect anything.
+func ChangedWorktreeFiles(
+	ctx context.Context,
+	worktreeRoot string,
+	commit plumbing.Hash,
+	paths []string,
+) (map[string]struct{}, error) {
+	changed := make(map[string]struct{})
+	if len(paths) == 0 {
+		return changed, nil
+	}
+
+	baseArgs := []string{
+		"--no-optional-locks", "-C", worktreeRoot,
+		"diff", "--name-only", "-z", "--no-renames", "--no-ext-diff", "--no-textconv",
+		commit.String(), "--",
+	}
+	for _, pathspecs := range chunkLiteralPathspecs(paths, gitDiffPathspecBudget) {
+		args := append(append([]string(nil), baseArgs...), pathspecs...)
+		cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", args...)
+		cmd.Env = EnvWithoutRepoOverrides()
+		out, err := cmd.Output()
+		if err != nil {
+			return nil, fmt.Errorf("git diff working tree against %s: %w", commit, err)
+		}
+
+		for entry := range bytes.SplitSeq(out, []byte{0}) {
+			if len(entry) != 0 {
+				changed[string(entry)] = struct{}{}
+			}
+		}
+	}
+	return changed, nil
+}
+
+// Keep pathspec argv comfortably below Windows' 32 KiB command-line limit,
+// including room for fixed arguments and os/exec quoting. Unix limits are much
+// larger. A single repository-relative path can exceed the budget and is sent
+// alone; filesystem path limits still keep that command bounded.
+const gitDiffPathspecBudget = 8 * 1024
+
+func chunkLiteralPathspecs(paths []string, budget int) [][]string {
+	var chunks [][]string
+	var (
+		chunk []string
+		size  int
+	)
+	for _, path := range paths {
+		pathspec := ":(literal)" + path
+		if len(chunk) > 0 && size+len(pathspec)+1 > budget {
+			chunks = append(chunks, chunk)
+			chunk = nil
+			size = 0
+		}
+		chunk = append(chunk, pathspec)
+		size += len(pathspec) + 1
+	}
+	if len(chunk) > 0 {
+		chunks = append(chunks, chunk)
+	}
+	return chunks
+}

+func TestChunkLiteralPathspecsBoundsCommandsWithoutDroppingPaths(t *testing.T) {
+	t.Parallel()
+
+	paths := []string{
+		strings.Repeat("a", 40),
+		strings.Repeat("b", 40),
+		strings.Repeat("c", 120), // A single path larger than the budget stays alone.
+		strings.Repeat("d", 40),
+	}
+	const budget = 100
+	chunks := chunkLiteralPathspecs(paths, budget)
+
+	var got []string
+	for _, chunk := range chunks {
+		var size int
+		for _, pathspec := range chunk {
+			got = append(got, strings.TrimPrefix(pathspec, ":(literal)"))
+			size += len(pathspec) + 1
+		}
+		if len(chunk) > 1 && size > budget {
+			t.Fatalf("multi-path chunk has size %d, budget %d", size, budget)
+		}
+	}
+	if !slices.Equal(got, paths) {
+		t.Fatalf("chunked paths = %q, want %q", got, paths)
+	}
+}

content.content:
- Each commit gets its own checkpoint ID (1:1 model)
- Both checkpoints link to the same session transcript

### Content-Aware Carry-Forward

The carry-forward logic uses **content-aware comparison** to determine which files have remaining uncommitted changes:

1. **File not in commit** → definitely has remaining changes
2. **File in commit, hash matches shadow branch** → fully committed, no carry-forward
3. **File in commit, hash differs from shadow branch** → partial commit (e.g., `git add -p`), carry forward

This enables splitting changes within a single file across multiple commits (see Scenario 7).

---

## Scenario 5: Partial Commit → Stash → Next Prompt

User commits some changes, stashes the rest, then runs another prompt.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant C as Claude
...

**A. Overlap Detection** (`filesOverlapWithContent`) - Determines if commit should be linked to session:
- Only applies to **newly created files**
- Modified files (existed in parent) **always count as overlap**
- Used in PrepareCommitMsg/PostCommit for non-ACTIVE sessions
- **Purpose**: Prevent linking commits where user reverted session content

**B. Carry-Forward Detection** (`filesWithRemainingAgentChanges`) - Determines which files to carry forward:
- Applies to **all committed files**
- Compares committed content hash vs shadow branch hash
- Hash mismatch = partial commit, file carried forward
- **Purpose**: Enable splitting changes within a file across commits (Scenario 7)

### 8. Carry-Forward Content Superseded by New Prompts

When files are carried forward and then a new prompt modifies the same file:
- The shadow branch gets the **new** content (from the new prompt's SaveChanges)
- The carried-forward content is overwritten
- Subsequent commits compare against the **new prompt's content**, not the original carried-forward content

**Example**:
1. Prompt 1: Agent writes 100 lines to file A
2. User commits 50 lines via `git add -p`
3. Carry-forward: A (with 100 lines) goes to new shadow branch
4. Prompt 2: Agent adds 50 more lines to A (now 150 lines total in worktree)
5. SaveChanges: Shadow branch now has A with 150 lines
=== line 436 ctx ===
    G->>G: remaining = []
    G->>SB: Condense checkpoint-2
    G->>S: FilesTouched = nil
```

### Key Points
- **Content-aware carry-forward**: Compares git blob hashes, not just filenames
- Partial staging (`git add -p`) within a single file is detected
- Each commit gets proper attribution, even when splitting one file's changes

content.text:
Reviewed all 5 commits. `mise run lint` is clean, `gitrepo` tests pass, and the autocrlf test is a genuine RED→GREEN (I ran the new tests against `main`'s `content_overlap.go` — `..._AutocrlfNormalizedWorkingTree` fails there). Two `strategy` failures exist (`TestSymlinkedHooksDirError_*`, macOS `/var` vs `/private/var`) but they're in untouched `hooks_test.go` and pre-existing.

The core change is right: `workingTreeMatchesBlob` compares raw disk bytes to a blob hash, so any clean filter — autocrlf, git-lfs, `ident`, a custom `filter.*.clean` — makes a clean file look permanently dirty and carry it forward forever. Delegating to git is the correct fix, and batching to one subprocess (fc12e7fad) beats the earlier per-file `--quiet --exit-code` design.

## 1. `--no-optional-locks` does not stop `git diff` from rewriting the index

This is the one I'd fix before merging. Measured on git 2.50.1 (Apple Git-155), same repo, same shape, stat-stale index:

| invocation | `.git/index` |
| --- | --- |
| `git status --porcelain` | REWRITTEN |
| `git --no-optional-locks status --porcelain` | UNCHANGED |
| `git diff --name-only HEAD -- <paths>` | REWRITTEN |
| `git --no-optional-locks diff --name-only HEAD -- <paths>` | **REWRITTEN** |
| `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0 git diff ...` (env form) | **REWRITTEN** |
| `git diff-index --name-only HEAD -- <paths>` | UNCHANGED |

`builtin/commit.c` gates its refresh on `use_optional_locks()`; `builtin/diff.c`'s `refresh_index_quietly()` doesn't. So `worktree_diff.go:33` carries the flag but still takes `.git/index.lock` and renames a new index over `.git/index` — the exact producer CLAUDE.md's "`git status` Is a Write" section documents (#2111: the `index.lock` collision with the user's own `git add`, and the virtiofs empty-tree commit), from the post-commit hook, asynchronous to the human's terminal.

It's not always-on: a fresh index → UNCHANGED. But the rewrite needs stat-stale entries, and this code only runs when there are candidates — committed content ≠ shadow content with a still-dirty worktree. That *is* the stat-stale case.

`git diff-index` avoids the write but reports stat-dirty-yet-content-identical files as changed. In this code that direction is conservative (an extra carry-forward, never a lost one), so it may be an acceptable trade — but it's a real behavior change, so it's your call. What shouldn't ship is the current state, where the flag reads as if it handles this and nothing says otherwise.

Related: `TestGitStatusCallSitesPassNoOptionalLocks` greps `"status"` only. This is the codebase's first worktree-comparing `git diff` — `experts_cmd.go:591` and `manual_commit_hooks.go:2840` are `--cached`, `review/scope.go:222` is `base...HEAD`, none touch the index. Whatever you decide, the guard should learn about `git diff <rev>` so the next call site doesn't rediscover this.

## 2. The fallback silently reinstates the bug, at Debug level

`content_overlap.go:527` — on timeout or any git failure the code drops to `workingTreeMatchesBlob`, which is filter-unaware by construction. In an lfs/autocrlf repo that's straight back to phantom carry-forward, and the only trace is a Debug line. `logging.Warn` matches how `StatusWalkBudget` breaches are surfaced.

Related: the 5s budget is an inline literal in the strategy layer. The convention here is a named budget beside the primitive (`gitrepo.StatusWalkBudget`); it belongs next to `ChangedWorktreeFiles`.

## 3. `ChangedWorktreeFiles` is never executed by a test

Only the pure `chunkLiteralPathspecs` helper is unit-tested. The multi-chunk merge inside `ChangedWorktreeFiles` is unreachable from any test — the strategy tests pass one path, and `gitDiffPathspecBudget` is a `const`, so nothing can force a second chunk. Making it a package `var` (or a parameter) would let one small `gitrepo` test cover the merge and the `:(literal)` claim in the doc comment. I did verify that claim by hand against real git — `:(literal)star*.txt` and `:(literal)sub/:(glob)weird.txt` both match exactly one file — so the comment is accurate, just unpinned.

## Smaller

- `worktree_diff.go:41` — `cmd.Output()` parks git's stderr in `ExitError.Stderr`, but `%w` renders only `exit status 128`. The Debug line in §2 will name no cause. `errors.As` + append `ee.Stderr`, or set `cmd.Stderr` to a buffer.
- `TestFilesWithRemainingAgentChanges_ComparesWorktreeToCommitNotIndex` passes on `main` too — it's a design pin against someone "simplifying" to a bare `git diff`, not a regression test. Worth saying so in its comment.
- `docs/architecture/checkpoint-scenarios.md:215-220` lists three carry-forward rules and never mentions the working-tree check at all. That gap predates this branch, but the branch changes that step from "raw blob hash" to "filter-aware", which is what CLAUDE.md means by keeping the docs current on strategy behavior.
- `testutil.InitRepo` already sets `core.autocrlf = true` in every test repo, so the explicit `config core.autocrlf true` at `content_overlap_test.go:428` is redundant. I'd keep it — it makes the test self-sufficient — but not everyone will read it that way.

## Checked and fine

`EnvWithoutRepoOverrides` is correctly applied (hook + `-C`, so `GIT_DIR`/`GIT_INDEX_FILE` would otherwise redirect it). `headTree` at `manual_commit_hooks.go:993` is `commit.Tree()`, so `headCommit.Hash` and `commitTree` can't disagree. The `keep []bool` rework preserves `filesTouched` ordering; `FilesTouched` is `omitempty`, so nil→empty slice is invisible in the state file and nothing nil-checks it. An unmatched pathspec exits 0 rather than erroring, and `git diff <commit>` correctly ignores a divergent index when the worktree matches the commit — both verified against real git.

content.text:
Re-reviewed at `ae39859f1`. The `git diff` approach is gone entirely, replaced by `git hash-object` — that's the right call, and it's a better answer than either option I named: it applies clean filters, never touches the index, and gives an exact hash so degradation can be per-file instead of all-or-nothing.

Verified fixed: `TestHashWorktreeFilesDoesNotRewriteStatStaleIndex` passes and I re-confirmed the mechanism by hand. Warn level, named `WorktreeContentHashBudget`, stderr in the error, real tests for the primitive, docs and CLAUDE.md updated, design-pin comment — all there. I also checked two things I'd have flagged otherwise and they're fine: custom clean filters really are applied (`filter.upper.clean` on a real repo hashes to the uppercased content, so the doc comment's claim holds beyond autocrlf), and `==` on `plumbing.Hash` is safe — go-git v6 declares `SHA1 ObjectFormat = iota`, so the zero `format` *is* SHA1 and `FromHex` sets SHA256 explicitly. It's stricter than `.Equal()`, which ignores the format field entirely, and stricter fails toward carry-forward.

Lint 0 issues; `gitrepo` passes; `strategy` has the same two pre-existing `TestSymlinkedHooksDirError_*` macOS `/var` failures in untouched `hooks_test.go`. The autocrlf test is still RED against `main`'s implementation.

## 1. The new guard is inert against the code it was written to prevent

I restored `f799fedc9`'s `worktree_diff.go` verbatim into the tree and ran `TestGitWorktreeDiffCallSitesDoNotRefreshTheIndex`. It **passes**.

`containsAnyMarker(rest)` requires a git-invocation marker on the same line as `"diff"`. gofmt puts a long argv on its own lines, so the file splits into:

```go
baseArgs := []string{
    "--no-optional-locks", "-C", worktreeRoot,
    "diff", "--name-only", "-z", ...   // ← "diff", no marker  → skipped
}
cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", args...)  // ← marker, no "diff" → never grepped
```

`git grep` does see the line (`--untracked` is on) — it's the marker requirement that drops it. The single-line form is caught; I confirmed that too with a throwaway `exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", "diff", "--name-only", "HEAD")`, which fails the guard correctly.

The status guard's documented limitation doesn't transfer, and that's the part worth internalizing. There, the flag and the word `"status"` both live on the argv line, so wrapping separates the *flag* from the word — a false positive, loud, safe. Here the marker lives on the `exec.Command` line and `"diff"` on the argv line, so wrapping separates the *marker* — a false negative, silent. Same structure, opposite failure direction.

Options: drop the marker requirement and match `"diff"` alone (noisier but sound), scan the enclosing statement rather than the line, or — matching existing precedent in this repo — an explicit `file:reason` allowlist like `entireDirCheckExemptions`, where anything unlisted fails.

Related and smaller: `strings.Contains(rest, `+"...HEAD"`)` matches one expression's exact gofmt spelling (`review/scope.go:222`). Rewriting it as `fmt.Sprintf("%s...HEAD", baseRef)`, or adding spaces around the `+`, fires the guard falsely. Loud direction, so not urgent.

## 2. Symlinks now always read as dirty

`git hash-object` follows the link and hashes the target's *content*; git stores a symlink blob as the target *path string*. Measured:

```
hash-object link.txt        → 9230cd37…   (content of real.txt)
git rev-parse HEAD:link.txt → c9c61fe1…   (hash of the string "real.txt")
```

So a symlink candidate can never compare clean — permanent carry-forward, the same phantom-loop class this branch exists to remove, for a narrow trigger. Not a regression against `main` (the raw-byte fallback also always said dirty), but it *is* one against the intermediate `git diff` version, which handled symlinks correctly. `commitTree.File(path)` already carries `Mode`, so skipping candidates with `filemode.Symlink` before the hash call is a couple of lines.

## 3. Smaller

- The Warn text says "using filter-unaware raw hashes for failed files", but for a missing or unreadable file the fallback isn't a raw-hash comparison at all — `ReadFileNoFollow` fails and the file is treated as dirty. Worth matching the wording to both outcomes.
- If `git` is off `$PATH`, the batch fails with a non-`ExitError`, `ctx.Err()` is nil, and the per-file retry spawns once per path; `errors.Join` then puts every one of those errors into a single Warn line. Bailing out of the retry when the batch error isn't an `ExitError` bounds it — the retry exists for "one bad file in a good batch", which is precisely the `ExitError` case.
- `--stdin-paths` would delete `chunkPaths`, its test, the 8 KiB budget and the Windows argv comment. I checked that it applies filters identically (`--stdin` implies `--no-filters`; `--stdin-paths` does not). You'd still need the per-file retry — git dies at the first bad path either way (verified: rc=128, partial stdout, stderr names the file). Purely optional.

One thing worth keeping: discarding the partial stdout on failure and retrying is the right call, and the `len(fields) != len(paths)` check is what makes it safe rather than merely cautious — git really does emit hashes for the files it processed before dying.

content.text:
Re-reviewed at `98b93c681`. All three findings landed, and I verified each by hand rather than by reading:

- **Guard** — I restored `f799fedc9`'s `worktree_diff.go` verbatim and the guard now **fails** on it (`worktree_diff.go:34`), where it previously passed. Stale-entry detection works too: commenting out the `review/scope.go` call produced `safe git diff allowlist entry is stale: cmd/entire/cli/review/scope.go`.
- **Symlinks** — routed to the confined path from *both* directions (commit mode `Symlink`, or a non-regular entry on disk), and `workingTreeMatchesBlob` now hashes the link target string, so a symlink can actually compare clean instead of being permanently dirty. The new test pins both directions.
- **Spawn failure** — `!errors.As(err, &exitErr)` skips the per-path retry, with a test. `t.Setenv` correctly means no `t.Parallel()`.

A side effect worth noticing: the `Lstat` prefilter means a missing file never reaches `git`, so the deleted-file case no longer produces a spurious Warn at all — better than the message rewording I asked for. `worktreedir.OpenAt` goes through `osroot.Shared`, so the per-candidate cost is a map lookup plus one `Lstat`.

Lint 0 issues; `gitrepo` passes; `strategy` has only the two pre-existing `TestSymlinkedHooksDirError_*` macOS `/var` failures in untouched `hooks_test.go`.

## One new thing: `IsRegular()` excludes Windows cloud placeholders

`requiresConfinedWorktreeHash` gates on `info.Mode().IsRegular()`. That's the right *shape* — `IsRegular` is `m&ModeType == 0`, a whole-field check, not the single-bit trap CLAUDE.md warns about — but `fs.ModeIrregular` is part of `ModeType` (confirmed: `ModeType&ModeIrregular != 0` is true, `ModeIrregular.IsRegular()` is false), and CLAUDE.md:639-658 records that Windows lands OneDrive Files On-Demand placeholders in exactly that bit, with a non-surrogate reparse tag so a placeholder file carries `ModeIrregular` alone.

If that holds, a repo inside a synced folder on Windows sends *no* candidate to `hash-object` — every one falls to the filter-unaware raw-byte path. Git for Windows defaults `core.autocrlf=true`, so the phantom carry-forward this branch exists to remove would persist for precisely the population most exposed to it, silently, with no warning (the file never reaches git, so nothing errors).

The repo already has the answer to this and it's two lines: `.entire`'s entry scan masks the bit rather than matching it — `mode.Type() &^ fs.ModeIrregular` must equal `0` or `ModeDir`. The same masking here (`info.Mode().Type() &^ fs.ModeIrregular != 0` → confined) keeps symlinks, FIFOs and directories out while letting a placeholder through.

I can't test this — I'm on darwin, and the claim rests on CLAUDE.md's own documented Windows finding rather than on a measurement I made. Worth a look before merge given the population it affects.

## Minor: the guard now fires on any `"diff"` string literal

Dropping the marker requirement is what fixed the wrapped-argv miss, and the comment says so — but it also means any non-git `"diff"` in `cmd/`/`internal/` fails the build. I confirmed with `var outputModes = map[string]int{"diff": 1, "json": 2}`, which produced "worktree-comparing git diff can rewrite the index even with --no-optional-locks" pointing at a map literal.

Loud and one line to fix, so the tradeoff is defensible; the message just doesn't admit the possibility. Adding "…or add an allowlist entry if this line is not a git invocation" would save the next person a minute. Related: the allowlist is keyed by path with a single fragment, so a file holding both a benign `"diff"` literal and a real git call can only exempt one of them.

Everything else I checked on this pass came back clean — `filemode.Symlink` on `commitFile.Mode`, the commit-Symlink-but-regular-on-disk and commit-Regular-but-symlink-on-disk crossings (both conservative), `chunkPaths(nil)` spawning nothing when every candidate is confined, and the `t.Setenv`/`t.Parallel` interaction in the new test.

content.text:
Re-reviewed at `2c662d152`. Both items are closed, and I verified each rather than reading for it.

**Cloud placeholders.** `requiresConfinedWorktreeMode` masks `ModeIrregular` out of the type field exactly as `.entire`'s entry scan does, and the table test pins the discriminating pairs — `ModeIrregular` alone passes, `ModeDir|ModeIrregular` and `ModeSymlink|ModeIrregular` still confine. Masking rather than matching is the right choice for the same reason CLAUDE.md gives: the substantive types stay rejected whatever else they carry.

Worth recording that the risk analysis here is *weaker* than the one that justified the precedent, not just equal to it. Bare `ModeIrregular` is ambiguous between a placeholder file and a junction, so masking does let a junction reach `hash-object` — but `hash-object` on a directory-like target just fails, which lands in the Warn-and-confine path. The outcome of getting it wrong is a clean/dirty verdict, not a read that goes anywhere; carry-forward's own content read is confined separately. So the "planting one already requires local code execution" argument has less to carry here than it does for `.entire`.

**Guard.** Slice-with-per-entry-`seen` works, and the three behaviors hold:

- wrapped argv (`f799fedc9`'s `worktree_diff.go` restored verbatim) → caught at line 34
- benign `map[string]int{"diff": 1}` → still fails, but the message now names the escape hatch
- stale entry → `...scope.go containing "baseRef+\"...HEAD\"" (compares two commits...)`, fragment included

One small asymmetry left in the staleness half only: `seen[i]` is set by any matching line, so two entries for the same file whose fragments both appear on one line would both be marked live, hiding a genuinely stale one. Safety is unaffected — that half fails a line that matches nothing.

**Checked and clear.** `TestWorkingTreeMatchesBlobSymlinkHashesTheTargetPath` calls `osroot.Shared` on a `t.TempDir()` under `t.Parallel()`, which is the shape that has caused cross-test breakage here before; nothing in the `strategy` package calls `osroot.ResetShared`, so there's no handle for it to pull out from under. `gitrepo` and the new `strategy` tests are stable at `-count=3 -race`.

Lint 0 issues. `gitrepo` green. `strategy` has only the two pre-existing `TestSymlinkedHooksDirError_*` macOS `/var` failures in untouched `hooks_test.go`.

Nothing further from me — every finding across the four passes is resolved, and the only thing I raised that wasn't taken is the optional `--stdin-paths` simplification, which is a judgment call rather than a defect.

Manage a trail's agent-native findings.

Running 'entire trail finding' shows the finding dashboard for the current
branch's trail. Pass a trail selector (number, id, or branch) to inspect another
trail in the same repo. Use 'entire trail list --status any' when you need to
discover a trail selector first.

      --json                Output as JSON

      --offset int          Pagination offset
      --severity string     Filter by comma-separated severity value(s): high,medium,low

Trail: Handle autocrlf in carry-forward detection
  Number:  1277
  ID:      01M23RT0YR2GAP7X0AMRZJ9BGT
  Branch:  soph/autocrlf-carry-forward-913
  Base:    main
  Status:  open

  Phase:   reviewing
  URL:     https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1277
  Assignees: Soph
  Type:      task
  Reviewers: gtrrz-victor (approved)
  Created: 2026-09-09T19:02:40Z
  Updated: 2026-09-10T13:45:52Z

Description:
Problem:
Carry-forward detection incorrectly identifies files for persistence when only line-ending differences exist. Git's core.autocrlf setting normalizes line endings transparently during read/write operations, so a file with committed LF can appear as CRLF on disk. The previous logic compared raw blob hashes, treating these normalized-only files as "changed" and marking them for carry-forward even when the working tree is intentionally clean.
Solution:
Added ChangedWorktreeFiles() in gitrepo to detect actual working-tree changes using native git diff, which respects git's clean filters. Carry-forward detection now batches file checks through this native command (with a 5-second timeout) to accurately determine which files truly differ, falling back to raw blob comparison only when git fails. The logic is renamed from workingTreeMatchesCommit to workingTreeMatchesBlob to clarify the fallback's filter-unaware nature. Tests verify that autocrlf-only differences don't create phantom carry-forward entries and that comparison is always against the commit, not the index.

Status:    open

Severity:  high

Location: cmd/entire/cli/gitrepo/worktree_hash.go:61-68

The context timeout is applied once at the start of `HashWorktreeFiles` but the retry loop in `hashWorktreeFiles` (lines 61-68) continues making individual `hashWorktreeFileBatch` calls even after `ctx` is canceled. This can exceed the `WorktreeContentHashBudget` by up to `len(batch) - 1` additional subprocess spawns, each blocking until killed by its own context. On a large batch (up to `gitHashObjectPathBudget / average_path_length` files), this multiplies the stated 5s budget. The fix is to check `ctx.Err() != nil` before entering the per-path retry loop at line 61, not just inside the loop termination condition at line 57.

Finding:   01M25RZ39QADJ8TMW5KK95FJQJ
Status:    open
Freshness: current
Severity:  low
Location: cmd/entire/cli/gitrepo/gitstatus_guard_test.go:112

The two guards in this file now make opposite trade-offs, and only the new one argues its case.

`TestGitStatusCallSitesPassNoOptionalLocks` filters candidate lines through `gitInvocationMarkers` and documents the wrapped-argv miss as the safe direction ("it fails loudly and the fix is to keep the argv on one line"). The new guard rejects exactly that reasoning and greps a bare `"diff"` with no marker.

Consequence: any future unrelated `"diff"` string literal under `cmd/`/`internal/` — a JSON tag, a map key, a subcommand name — fails the build with a message about index rewriting, and the remedy is an entry in a list called `safeGitDiffCalls` whose `reason` field is shaped for worktree-reading semantics ("compares the index to HEAD and never reads the worktree"). The list would then hold two different kinds of entry.

Cost is zero today — there are exactly 3 such lines and all 3 are real git invocations, and I confirmed all 3 allowlist reasons are empirically accurate (index-only, two-tree, and three-dot diffs all leave a stat-stale index alone; the worktree-comparing form rewrites it even under `--no-optional-locks`, on 2.55.0 as well as the 2.50.1 in the doc). The error text also already anticipates the non-git case.

The worry: the next person to hit a false positive has to reconstruct why the marker filter was skipped here but kept 100 lines up. One sentence saying it was considered and why the false-positive direction was preferred would settle it.

════════ 01M25RYQ85J3 ════════
Finding:   01M25RYQ85J37B876Y203B0NZZ
Status:    open
Freshness: current
Severity:  low
Location: cmd/entire/cli/gitrepo/worktree_hash.go:106

The comment justifies *batching* ("an oversized argv cannot fail before Git inspects anything") but not argv-vs-stdin, which is the question a reviewer actually arrives with: why not delete `chunkPaths` and its test and use `git hash-object --stdin-paths`?

There is a real answer and it is not in the file. `hash-object` has no `-z`, so `--stdin-paths` is newline-separated only:

    $ printf 'we\nird.txt\n' | git hash-object --stdin-paths
    fatal: could not open 'we' for reading: No such file or directory
    $ git hash-object -- $'we\nird.txt'
    587be6b4c3f93f93c489c0111bba5596147a26cb

Git paths can contain newlines, so argv is the more correct form, not the fussier one. (`--stdin-paths` does apply clean filters, so that half is not the reason.)

The worry: the batching reads like scaffolding a simplifier can remove, and the change would look like a clean win right up to the first path with a newline in it.

════════ 01M25RXMC3F4 ════════
Finding:   01M25RXMC3F4AXP006507P86KN
Status:    open
Freshness: current
Severity:  low
Location: cmd/entire/cli/strategy/content_overlap.go:536

The native path compares hashes with `==`; the fallback three lines down (line 629) uses `commitHash.Equal(h.Sum())`. Those are not the same operation. `ObjectID.Equal` is `bytes.Equal(s.hash[:], in.hash[:])` — the 32-byte array only. `==` compares the whole struct, including the `format` field, whose zero value is `UnsetObjectFormat` (""), not `SHA1`.

It works today. I probed both object formats against this repo's go-git version — a sha1 repo and a `git init --object-format=sha256` repo — and `NewHash(treeHash.String()) == treeHash` was true in both, because `FromHex` and go-git's tree decoder happen to agree on leaving 40-char hashes unset and stamping 64-char ones SHA256.

The worry: go-git is on `v6.0.0-alpha.5`. If a decoder ever starts stamping `format: "sha1"` while `FromHex` keeps leaving it unset, `==` goes silently false, every candidate reads dirty, and the phantom carry-forward this branch fixes comes back — with no test failing, since nothing here pins the format field. `.Equal` is immune and is what the function already uses on the other branch.

The comment justifies *batching* ("an oversized argv cannot fail before Git inspects anything") but not argv-vs-stdin, which is the question a reviewer actually arrives with: why not delete `chunkPaths` and its test and use `git hash-object --stdin-paths`?

There is a real answer and it is not in the file. `hash-object` has no `-z`, so `--stdin-paths` is newline-separated only:

    $ printf 'we\nird.txt\n' | git hash-object --stdin-paths
    fatal: could not open 'we' for reading: No such file or directory
    $ git hash-object -- $'we\nird.txt'
    587be6b4c3f93f93c489c0111bba5596147a26cb

Git paths can contain newlines, so argv is the more correct form, not the fussier one. (`--stdin-paths` does apply clean filters, so that half is not the reason.)

The worry: the batching reads like scaffolding a simplifier can remove, and the change would look like a clean win right up to the first path with a newline in it.

content.text:
Five findings on trail #1277, but `entire trail finding list` shows three — the default `--freshness current` hides the only High one. Full picture with `--freshness any --status any --include-dismissed`.

## The hidden High is obsolete, and its mechanism is wrong

`01M23YTRSN2H` (high, 0.95, stale) — claims the retry loop keeps spawning subprocesses after `ctx` is cancelled, "each blocking until killed by its own context", multiplying the 5s budget, and prescribes checking `ctx.Err()` before the retry loop.

That check is already there — `worktree_hash.go:59`, ahead of the retry loop at :63; commit `98b93c681` added it. And the mechanism doesn't hold anyway: `exec.Cmd.Start` returns `ctx.Err()` before forking, so calls under a dead context cost nothing. Measured 500 of them at **11.8ms total, zero processes started**, against ~11ms each for a live context. No budget multiplication is reachable.

What's left is cosmetic: if the context expires *during* a retry loop, every remaining path appends an error and `errors.Join` puts them all in one Warn line. Log noise, not a budget breach.

## Two of the current findings are substantive, and one corrects me

**`01M25RXMC3F4` — `==` vs `.Equal` on `plumbing.Hash`. This one is right and I was wrong.** Last review I told you `==` was safe because go-git declares `SHA1 ObjectFormat = iota`, so the zero `format` is SHA1. That came from the wrong module directory — my `ls | head -1` picked an older cached copy. The version this repo actually pins (`v6.0.0-alpha.5.0.20260812155443`) has:

```go
type ObjectFormat string
UnsetObjectFormat ObjectFormat = ""
SHA1              ObjectFormat = "sha1"
```

So the zero value is `""`, not SHA1, exactly as the finding says. I probed both formats against the pinned version:

```
sha1(default)  tree.format=""       fromHex.format=""       ==:true  Equal:true
sha256         tree.format="sha256" fromHex.format="sha256" ==:true  Equal:true
```

It works only because the tree decoder and `FromHex` happen to agree on leaving 40-char hashes unset. `Equal` ignores `format` entirely and is immune; the fallback three lines down already uses it. On an alpha dependency, with nothing pinning the format field, that's a real asymmetry worth closing — and my earlier "checked and clear" on it shouldn't be relied on.

**`01M25RYQ85J3` — argv vs `--stdin-paths`.** Also a direct rebuttal of something I suggested (twice). Verified: `git hash-object` has no `-z`, `--stdin-paths` is newline-delimited only, and a path containing a newline breaks it while argv handles it:

```
$ printf 'we\nird.txt\n' | git hash-object --stdin-paths
fatal: could not open 'we' for reading: No such file or directory
$ git hash-object -- $'we\nird.txt'
587be6b4c3f93f93c489c0111bba5596147a26cb
```

So `chunkPaths` is the correct design, not scaffolding — and the file doesn't say why, which is the finding's actual point. Withdraw my `--stdin-paths` suggestion.

## The rest

`01M25RZ39QAD` (low, current) — documentation only: the two guards in `gitstatus_guard_test.go` now take opposite positions on the marker filter and only the new one argues its case. Same ground as the benign-`"diff"`-literal note I raised; the ask is one sentence saying the false-positive direction was chosen deliberately. The finding confirms all three allowlist reasons are empirically accurate, on git 2.55.0 as well as the 2.50.1 in the doc.

`01M25RXY2WDP` (dismissed) — verbatim duplicate of `01M25RYQ85J3`, anchored at `whole_change` instead of a file:line.

Net: two worth acting on (`==` → `.Equal`, and a comment explaining argv-over-stdin), one one-liner comment, one obsolete-and-incorrect High. Want me to apply the two code-level ones, and resolve the stale High with a note on why — or leave the trail alone?

**`content_overlap.go:536`** — `worktreeHash == candidate.commitHash` → `worktreeHash.Equal(candidate.commitHash)`, with a comment naming the format field as the reason. Description:
Problem:
Carry-forward detection incorrectly identifies files for persistence when only line-ending differences exist. Git's core.autocrlf setting normalizes line endings transparently during read/write operations, so a file with committed LF can appear as CRLF on disk. The previous logic compared raw blob hashes, treating these normalized-only files as "changed" and marking them for carry-forward even when the working tree is intentionally clean.
Solution:
Added ChangedWorktreeFiles() in gitrepo to detect actual working-tree changes using native git diff, which respects git's clean filters. Carry-forward detection now batches file checks through this native command (with a 5-second timeout) to accurately determine which files truly differ, falling back to raw blob comparison only when git fails. The logic is renamed from workingTreeMatchesCommit to workingTreeMatchesBlob to clarify the fallback's filter-unaware nature. Tests verify that autocrlf-only differences don't create phantom carry-forward entries and that comparison is always against the commit, not the index.

`filesWithRemainingAgentChanges` compared the clean-filtered worktree hash against the commit blob hash with `==`. `plumbing.Hash` is a struct carrying an object-format field alongside its bytes, and `==` compares that field too:

	hash   [format.SHA256Size]byte
	format format.ObjectFormat // "" | "sha1" | "sha256"
}

func (s ObjectID) Equal(in ObjectID) bool { return bytes.Equal(s.hash[:], in.hash[:]) }

sha256         tree.format="sha256" fromHex.format="sha256" ==:true  Equal:true
```

So it works today, by coincidence. If a decoder ever stamped `"sha1"` while `FromHex` kept leaving it unset, every candidate would compare dirty, the phantom carry-forward #2336 fixed would come back, and nothing would fail — no test pins the format field. `.Equal` ignores it by construction and is already what the fallback branch three lines down uses.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, indefinitely** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Timeout → killed. Set `persistent: true` for session-length watches (PR monitoring, log tails) — the monitor runs until you call TaskStop or the session ends. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms, max 3600000ms. Ignored when persistent is true.

persistent.description: Run for the lifetime of the session (no timeout). Use for session-length watches like PR monitoring or log tails. Stop with TaskStop.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

cat > "$SP/commit-msg.txt" <<'MSG'
Compare carry-forward hashes with Equal, not ==

plumbing.Hash is a struct carrying an object-format field alongside its bytes, so == compares that field too. FromHex stamps sha256 on a 64-char hash and leaves the field unset on a 40-char one, which means == holds only while go-git's tree decoder makes the same choice. Probed against the pinned v6.0.0-alpha.5.0.20260812155443, it does — sha1 gives "" on both sides, sha256 gives "sha256" on both — so this works today by coincidence. If a decoder ever stamped "sha1", every candidate would compare dirty, the phantom carry-forward #2336 fixed would return, and nothing would fail, because no test pins the format field. Equal ignores it by construction and is already what the fallback branch three lines down uses.

Also records two decisions reviewers reached independently. hash-object takes its paths as argv rather than --stdin-paths because hash-object has no -z, so --stdin-paths is newline-delimited and splits a legal path containing a newline into two nonexistent ones; the chunking that supports argv is therefore not scaffolding to be removed. And TestGitWorktreeDiffCallSitesDoNotRefreshTheIndex drops the gitInvocationMarkers filter that TestGitStatusCallSitesPassNoOptionalLocks keeps because the failure direction inverts between them: a wrapped argv separates the flag from "status" (loud false positive) but would separate the marker from "diff" (silent false negative).

Follow-up to #2336; resolves findings on trail 1277.

content.text:
PR open: **https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2372** — `soph/carry-forward-hash-equal-followup` → `main`, one commit (`65f0e2959`), and I verified the `.Equal` line is actually on the pushed branch rather than just locally.

**Contents** — the three changes that missed the #2336 merge: `==` → `.Equal` at `content_overlap.go:542` (the only behavior change), plus the `--stdin-paths` rationale in `worktree_hash.go` and the guard trade-off rationale in `gitstatus_guard_test.go`.

**Verification.** `mise run fmt && mise run lint` clean, then `mise run test:ci` green with the real exit code — `cli/strategy ok (125s)`, no FAIL lines, no data races. `TestFilesWithRemainingAgentChanges_AutocrlfNormalizedWorkingTree` is the one that actually exercises the swap: it needs the comparison to return *true* for a clean file, so it would fail if `.Equal` were wrong in either direction.

Two things caught along the way that were worth the extra loop:

- **The first test run's green was fake.** I'd piped `mise run test:ci` through `tail`, so the exit code I saw was `tail`'s, not mise's — and `test:ci` is two commands, so a unit-stage failure could have hidden behind the canary's success. Re-ran capturing the real status. It was genuinely 0, but it wasn't yet evidence when I first reported it.
- **`git checkout -b … origin/main` set the new branch's upstream to `origin/main`**, so a bare `git push` would have gone straight at main. Pushed with an explicit refspec; upstream now points at the new remote branch.

Also of note: the two `TestSymlinkedHooksDirError_*` `/var` failures I'd been treating as a standing environmental fact don't reproduce under `-tags=integration -race` — they only showed up in my plain `go test` runs. So that's narrower than I'd been describing it.

Trail #1277's four findings were already resolved yesterday; the code backing three of them now has a PR, so that mismatch closes when this merges.

content.text:
Probed every public construction path against the repo's own pinned go-git. This changes the picture, including something I told you wrong.

```
NewHash(40hex)="" FromHex(40hex)="" ResetBySize(SHA1Size)="" NewHasher(SHA1).Sum()=""
cross-source (==)=true   cross-source (Equal)=true
```

**Nothing in `v6.0.0-alpha.5.0.20260812155443` ever produces a `"sha1"`-stamped hash.** `Sum()` explicitly normalises non-SHA256 to unset (`hash.go:58-63`), and `ResetBySize` does the same (`objectid.go:151`). The format field is determined purely by size — 64-hex → `"sha256"`, everything else → `""` — so two hashes of the same object in one repo always agree, and `==` cannot diverge from `.Equal` at this version. The divergence is unreachable, not merely unlikely.

## Copilot (PR #2372, one inline comment)

> reverting this line to `==` would still make the test pass … otherwise the specific format-mismatch behavior this change protects is not pinned

**Correct, and it catches an overclaim of mine.** I told you the autocrlf test "would fail if `.Equal` were wrong in either direction." It wouldn't — it passes with both operators, because both sides carry `""`. It proves the comparison works; it does not pin format-independence.

Where I'd push back is on the remedy. The test Copilot asks for isn't constructible: I enumerated every public constructor above and none yields a `"sha1"` stamp, so there's no way to hand `filesWithRemainingAgentChanges` two hashes with equal bytes and different formats. The property can only be pinned at the call sites, not through behaviour.

## Trail #1305 — seven findings, all the same class

Two High in the file I edited, five Medium elsewhere. My own `git grep` found **eight** sites (the trail missed `checkpointpolicy/remote.go:284`):

```
content_overlap.go:168          headFile.Hash == shadowFile.Hash
content_overlap.go:497          commitFile.Hash == shadowFile.Hash
checkpointpolicy/remote.go:104  local.Hash == baseline.Hash
checkpointpolicy/remote.go:190  local.Hash == remoteState.Hash

checkpointpolicy/update.go:61   local.Hash == baseline.Hash
resume.go:683                   current.Hash == *stopAt
manual_commit_opf_rewrite.go:522 c.Hash == remoteTip
```

The finding is right that my fix was partial — I changed only the line the original finding named and left one 45 lines above it in the same function. But the High rating and "phantom carry-forward would return" don't hold: by the probe above, none of these can diverge today, including the one I changed. This is a consistency-and-robustness class, not a live bug in any of the eight.

## What I'd do

Fix all eight and add a `testutil.GitGrepGuard` source guard, in the style of the four the repo already has. That's the real answer to Copilot: since the behaviour can't be exercised, the convention has to be pinned at the call sites, and a guard does that for future ones too — which a unit test never would. Fixing only the two in `content_overlap.go` would leave the guard needing a five-entry allowlist, so all eight is actually the simpler change.

Done — PR #2372 now has two commits, all seven findings resolved, PR description updated for the expanded scope.

## What landed in `83fc621ff`

All eight `.Hash ==` sites converted to `.Equal`, including `checkpointpolicy/remote.go:284` that the review pass missed, plus `TestHashComparisonsUseEqual` — a `testutil.GitGrepGuard` source guard in the style of the four the repo already has.

The guard is the answer to Copilot's comment, and its doc comment says why it's a guard rather than the test that was asked for: I probed `NewHash`, `FromHex`, `ResetBySize` and `Hasher.Sum` against the pinned go-git and all leave the format field unset for a 40-char hash, so a format mismatch is unconstructible through the public API. No assertion can distinguish the two operators — a reverted call site stays green. I verified the guard the only way that means anything, by reverting `content_overlap.go:497` and watching it fail, then restoring it.

`mise run test:ci` green with the real exit code — `strategy` 115s, `gitrepo` 12s, `checkpointpolicy` 9s, no failures, no data races.

## Two corrections carried into the record

Both went into the commit message, the PR body and the finding resolutions rather than just being mentioned here:

**Copilot was right and I was wrong.** I'd claimed the autocrlf regression covers the `.Equal` change. It doesn't — it passes with either operator.

**The findings' severity was overstated.** They rated the `content_overlap.go` ones High with "phantom carry-forward would return." Nothing was reachable: at the pinned version two hashes of the same object in one repo always carry the same format, so `==` could not diverge at any of the eight sites. It's hardening against a dependency change pinned at an alpha, not a bug fix — worth doing, but I said so rather than accepting the framing.

## Two things left for you

**The ZeroHash family is unfiled.** Twelve `== plumbing.ZeroHash` comparisons. The operator genuinely diverges there — `NewHash(64 zeros) == ZeroHash` is false while `IsZero()` is true — which is more than can be said for the sha1 family, and it's the reason the new guard deliberately doesn't cover it. But I traced the sites and found no path that reaches a sha256 zero hash; `reftable.go:313`, the likeliest, already uses `IsZero()`. So it's latent too, and I didn't file it rather than file it overstated.

**I haven't replied to Copilot's comment.** Posting to the PR isn't something I do unasked. Say the word and I'll post the unconstructibility finding as a reply, since it's the part that explains why the requested test doesn't exist.
